original_note: title_bis "78 Ethanol Kulob" for "Ethanol Boils 78 Celsius". *Kulob* again replaces *bukal*; the body is correct ("mobukal sa mga 78 degrees Celsius"). The headline gives a number with no process word a Cebuano child can read as boiling. Duplicate bad title also on ffct-19421.
fact_en: Ethanol, which is a type of alcohol, boils at about 78 degrees Celsius (78°C). It boils at a lower temperature than plain water!
fact_bis: Ang ethanol, nga matang sa alkohol, mobukal sa mga 78 degrees Celsius (78°C). Mobukal kini sa mas ubos nga temperatura kay sa ordinaryong tubig!

original_note: title_bis 'Kalawang sa Pako sa Bakal' = 'rust on the iron WING'. Cebuano pako = wing (Tagalog false friend: pako = nail in TL); nail is lansang. Body repeats 'ang mga pako sa gawas' / 'ang mga pako nga puthaw' and never says lansang, so the object rusting is never recoverable from the Cebuano.
fact_en:
Why do iron nails turn brown and flaky outside?

When exposed to oxygen and moisture in the air, iron nails chemically react to form flaky brown rust!
fact_bis:
Nganong nagiging kayumanggi ug nagkakaroon og kalawang ang mga pako sa gawas?

Kung ma-expose sa oxygen ug moisture sa hangin, mo-react ang mga pako nga puthaw ug maghimo og kayumanggi nga kalawang!

original_note: EN: "Oil floats on water during a kitchen grease fire." BIS says "motunaw ang mantika sa tubig" = the oil MELTS/DISSOLVES in the water. That is the opposite of the fact and is itself false (another card in this same batch, ffct-20054, correctly says "Dili mag-uban ang lana ug tubig"). The Cebuano-only child is left with no reason why water must never be used: floating oil spreading the flame is the whole point, and nothing else on the card restores it. Correct word is molutaw.
fact_en: Oil floats on water during a kitchen grease fire, so you must never use water to extinguish it!
fact_bis: Sa kusina, motunaw ang mantika sa tubig kung naay grease fire, mao nga dili dapat gamiton ang tubig aron patyon kini!

original_note: title_bis "Sabon nga Kape sa Lana" for "Soap Binds to Grease" — `kape` is COFFEE in Cebuano. The headline a child sees reads "Soap that is Coffee in Oil"; coffee is nowhere in the card and the binding verb (body uses `makakupot`) is missing from the title entirely. Looks like a garble of kapot/kupot (to grip/cling).
fact_en: Soap cleans grease off your hands because its molecules bind to both water and oil, washing the dirt away!
fact_bis: Ang sabon mopahaw sa grasa sa imong kamot kay ang mga molekula niini makakupot sa tubig ug lana, maong mawala ang hugaw!

original_note: Relationship reversed: EN says vinegar is too acidic for spoilage bacteria to SURVIVE; BIS says 'Aslom kaayo ang suka AroN MABUHI ang kadaghanan sa bakterya' = 'sour enough so that most bacteria CAN LIVE'. The 'dili' is missing, so the Cebuano-only child learns the opposite of the card's single fact, and the trailing 'kay molungtad ang pagkaon' (because the food lasts) inverts cause and effect too. Nothing elsewhere on the card restores it. Aggravating: 'nagpapabulok' is Tagalog morphology and in Cebuano 'bulok' does not mean rotten, so the spoilage idea is also lost (Cebuano would be 'makapap
fact_en:
Why do pickled vegetables and vinegar-soaked foods last so long?

Vinegar is too acidic for most spoilage bacteria to survive — so the food stays fresh longer!
fact_bis:
Ngano molungtad og dugay ang atsara ug mga pagkaong gibabad sa suka?

Aslom kaayo ang suka aron mabuhi ang kadaghanan sa bakterya nga nagpapabulok — kay molungtad ang pagkaon!

original_note: title_bis "100 Pirmi Kulob" — kulob means face-down/overturned in Cebuano, not boiling (bukal). The headline of a boiling-point card contains no word for boiling; body is correct ("nagbukal nga tubig"). Systemic: 29 titles use kulob for boiling (ffct-15225, ffct-16213, ffct-16221 '212 Fahrenheit Kulob'), and the same word is also used for 'wrinkle' in ffct-02691, which shows it is a confused token rather than a regional variant.
fact_en:
Why does boiling water stay at 100 degrees Celsius?

The extra heat doesn't raise the temperature — it goes into turning the water into steam!
fact_bis:
Ngano nga magpabilin sa mga 100 degrees Celsius ang nagbukal nga tubig?

Wala nay init nga modugang sa temperature — mopaingon kini sa pag-usab sa tubig ngadto sa alisngaw!

original_note: Body: "Ang paghigop sa DAYAMI nagpaubos sa air pressure sa sulod" for EN "Sucking on a straw". dayami/dagami = rice straw, i.e. HAY — the wrong sense of the English homonym. A drinking straw is straw/sipsipan/tubo. The whole card is about the drinking straw as the object, and the Cebuano never names it, so a child learns the atmospheric-pressure mechanism attached to a stalk of hay. Bad pair is also baked into terms ("straw,dayami").
fact_en: Sucking on a straw reduces air pressure inside it. The higher atmospheric pressure outside then pushes the liquid right up into your mouth!
fact_bis: Ang paghigop sa dayami nagpaubos sa air pressure sa sulod. Ang mas taas nga atmospheric pressure sa gawas ang nagtulod sa likido pataas!

original_note: title_bis "Dayami sa Kuryente" names rice STRAW (the stalks), not the rice HULL/chaff (ipa/tahop) the card is about — a different agricultural material, and it is the headline a child sees. The body correctly uses and even defines "ipa sa bigas", so the science fact survives, but the title equates dayami with ipa and never corrects it; title should be e.g. "Ipa sa Bigas ug Kuryente".
fact_en:
Did you know rice hulls can make electricity?

The rice hull is the outer shell removed from grain during milling. It can be burned to produce heat and electricity in biomass plants in the Philippines' rice-farming areas!
fact_bis:
Nahibaw-an ba nimo nga ang ipa sa bigas makahimo ug kuryente?

Ang ipa sa bigas mao ang gawas nga balat nga giwagtang sa panahon sa pag-mills. Mahimong kini sunogon aron makahimo ug init ug kuryente sa mga biomass plant sa mga lugar nga may daghang palayan sa Pilipinas!

original_note: "Kung ibutang ang DAYAMI sa baso sa tubig" plus title_bis 'Kurbado nga Dayami'. dayami = rice straw/hay, not a drinking straw (istro/straw); the English polysemy was resolved the wrong way. Both title and body use it and nothing corrects it, so the child is told to put hay in a glass of water rather than the drinking straw the demonstration depends on.
fact_en: When you put a straw in a glass of water, it looks bent at the surface! This happens because light refracts as it passes from water into air.
fact_bis: Kung ibutang ang dayami sa baso sa tubig, murag nakabiko kini sa ibabaw! Mahitabo kini tungod sa refraction sa suga gikan sa tubig ngadto sa hangin.

original_note: "Sa BAKAL ang tunog mobalhin og mga 5,100 m/s" — bakal = TO BUY in Cebuano; steel/iron is puthaw or landok. This is the sentence that carries the 5,100 m/s figure, so the number is attached to a verb ('in buying') rather than a material. Only the keyword title ('Tunog Malaksi Landok Solido') has the right word — weak repair for the load-bearing fact sentence.
fact_en: Sound travels faster in solids and liquids than in air! In steel, sound moves at about 5,100 m/s, compared to about 343 m/s in air.
fact_bis: Mas dali ang tunog sa mga solid ug liquid kaysa sa hangin! Sa bakal ang tunog mobalhin og mga 5,100 m/s, kumpara sa mga 343 m/s sa hangin.

original_note: "wool" is rendered "lana" in BOTH the title ("Lana Hangin Insulator") and the body question ("Nganong ang lana ug nakulong nga hangin nagpabilin og mainit?"). In Cebuano lana = COCONUT OIL (Tagalog lana = wool); Cebuano wool is balhibo sa karnero / delana. The card never says wool anywhere, and the follow-up "gigamit kini sa damit ug bubong sa balay" reinforces the false reading: a child learns that OIL is a great insulator used in clothing and roofing. Nothing in the card restores wool.
fact_en:
Why do wool and trapped air keep us warm?

They're poor conductors of heat, making them great insulators! That's why they're used in clothing and roof insulation to keep buildings warm or cool inside.
fact_bis:
Nganong ang lana ug nakulong nga hangin nagpabilin og mainit?

Dili maayong conductor sa init, nagahimo kanila nga maayo nga insulator! Kaya gigamit kini sa damit ug bubong sa balay aron mapabilin ang mainit o malamig ang sulod.
